title: Norfolk Southern Railway v. State Corporation Commission
description: Whether Code § 56-16.3, which permits private broadband service providers to install fiber optic cables across railroad property, constitutes an unconstitutional taking of private property for a nonpublic use under Article I, Section 11 of the Constitution of Virginia.
plaintiff_argument: Norfolk Southern argued that Code § 56-16.3 violates the Virginia Constitution by allowing a private, for-profit company (Cox) to take its property for a nonpublic use and by eliminating the condemnor's burden to establish public use.
defendant_argument: The State Corporation Commission, siding with Cox, asserted that Norfolk Southern's claims were insufficient to establish an "undue hardship" and that the statute was intended to promote broadband expansion, which is a public interest.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the State Corporation Commission, holding that Code § 56-16.3, as applied, violates Article I, Section 11 of the Constitution of Virginia by permitting a private company to take railroad property for a nonpublic use.

title: Layla H v. Virginia
description: Whether the Commonwealth of Virginia's policies and statutes for fossil fuel permitting violate the plaintiffs' jus publicum and constitutional rights due to climate change, with plaintiffs arguing these policies cause climate change and infringe on their rights, and the Commonwealth arguing the claims are barred by sovereign immunity and plaintiffs lack standing.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth's policy and practice of approving fossil fuel infrastructure permits cause and contribute to climate change, which substantially impairs their jus publicum rights and violates their constitutional rights to life, liberty, and property.
defendant_argument: The plaintiffs' claims are barred by sovereign immunity, they lack standing because their alleged injuries are not justiciable, the relief sought would not redress their injuries, and the alleged injuries were not caused by the defendants.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' complaint with prejudice, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked standing and that their jus publicum claims were barred by sovereign immunity, while clarifying that Article I, § 11 claims are not barred by sovereign immunity.

title: Vlaming v. West Point School Board
description: Whether the West Point School Board's termination of a French teacher for refusing to use a transgender student's preferred masculine pronouns, due to religious beliefs, violated the teacher's constitutional and statutory rights.
plaintiff_argument: Vlaming claims he lost his job because his conscience would not allow him to use government-mandated pronouns, which he believed would violate his sincerely held religious beliefs against intentionally lying about gender identity. He used the student's preferred name and avoided third-person pronouns.
defendant_argument: The School Board terminated Vlaming for refusing to use masculine pronouns for a transgender student and for refusing to comply with directives, which they stated violated School Board policies prohibiting discrimination and harassment based on gender identity.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed the circuit court's dismissal of Vlaming's claims, finding them legally viable and remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: McKeithen v. City of Richmond
description: Whether Code § 58.1-3967, which directs unclaimed surplus proceeds from a tax sale to the City after its tax lien is satisfied, unconstitutionally infringes upon the property rights of a partially satisfied junior lienor.
plaintiff_argument: The Caldwell Trust argued that the unclaimed surplus proceeds from the tax sale, originally designated for a superior lienor who forfeited their claim, should be applied to its outstanding debt, and that the statute's application to give these funds to the City violates constitutional property rights.
defendant_argument: The City of Richmond argued that under Code § 58.1-3967, the unclaimed portion of the surplus proceeds escheats to the City, even though its tax lien was fully satisfied, and that the Caldwell Trust had no property interest in those specific funds.
decision_outcome: The court held that the escheat provision of Code § 58.1-3967, as applied to the factual circumstances of this case, violates Article I, Section 11 of the Constitution of Virginia, and reversed and remanded the circuit court's decision.

title: Anderson v. Clarke
description: Whether Antoine Anderson is eligible for enhanced earned sentence credits (ESCs) under HB 5148 retroactively, or if Item 404(R)(2) of the 2022 Appropriation Act correctly limits his ESCs to 4.5 per 30 days due to his disqualifying offense, and whether this limitation violates constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: Anderson argued that VDOC misapplied Item 404(R)(2) by limiting his ESCs to 4.5 per 30 days for time served before July 1, 2022, contending he was entitled to up to 15 ESCs under HB 5148 retroactively, and that VDOC's interpretation violated ex post facto and due process clauses.
defendant_argument: The defendant (VDOC) argued that HB 5148 and Item 404(R)(2) must be read together, establishing that Anderson was entitled to a maximum of 4.5 ESCs per 30 days served due to his disqualifying offense, and that this interpretation did not violate any constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the circuit court, denying Antoine Anderson's petition for a writ of habeas corpus.

title: Taylor v. Northam
description: Whether language in an 1890 deed and an 1889 joint resolution prohibits the Governor of Virginia from ordering the removal of a state-owned monument from state-owned property.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the 1889 Joint Resolution and the 1890 Deed created enforceable restrictive covenants requiring the Commonwealth to perpetually maintain the Lee Monument, and that the Governor's order to remove it violated the Virginia Constitution and public policy.
defendant_argument: The Governor argued he had the authority to remove the monument, that the deeds' language was not an enforceable restrictive covenant, and even if it was, it violated public policy by forcing the Commonwealth to express a message it disagreed with.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, concluding that the purported restrictive covenants were unenforceable and the Governor's order to remove the Lee Monument did not violate the Constitution of Virginia, thereby dissolving all injunctions against the monument's removal.
